strengths: Clear motivation and conceptually clean framework: Shifting from learning context-agnostic compression tokens from scratch (which heavily depend on autoencoding reconstruction) to selecting contextual anchor tokens with bidirectional attention and anchor embeddings is intuitive, effective, and well-justified.

Training efficiency: Bypassing the autoencoding reconstruction objective shortens pretraining time by ~26-31% while yielding lower language modeling perplexity and faster supervised finetuning convergence.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated on both in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA benchmark tasks across multiple compression ratios (5x, 15x, and 51x), showing consistent gains over strong recent baselines like ICAE, 500xCompressor, and EPL.

Thorough ablation studies and analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations on anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention, token selection schemes, and training objectives (AE vs. LM), alongside helpful t-SNE and attention map visualizations that elucidate the representational alignment.
weaknesses: Evaluations are restricted to a single, small model: All experiments are performed on Llama-3.2-1B. Demonstrating applicability to larger and more widely used open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B) is important for establishing scalability in context compression.

Narrow benchmark diversity: The evaluation relies exclusively on the MRQA question-answering benchmark. Context compression methods typically benefit from evaluation across diverse long-context capabilities, such as long-form summarization, multi-hop reasoning, and retrieval benchmarks (e.g., LongBench, L-Eval, or RULER).

Missing inference efficiency profiling: While pretraining wall-clock speedup is documented in the appendix, the paper lacks end-to-end inference metrics (e.g., encoding latency, memory footprint, time-to-first-token, and throughput) across different sequence lengths and compression ratios compared to uncompressed inference.

strengths: The core idea of bypassing explicit autoencoding pretraining by designating in-situ contextual anchor tokens with bidirectional attention is intuitive, technically straightforward, and computationally advantageous (reducing pretraining time by ~26-31%).

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive within the MRQA suite, comparing against multiple strong soft compression baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL) and hard compression (LLMLingua-2) across six in-domain and six out-of-domain datasets at varying compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x).

The ablation studies and analytical sections (attention map visualizations, t-SNE feature space analysis, ablation of bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, and selection strategies) effectively isolate the contribution of each design component.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single, small model size (Llama-3.2-1B). Context compression techniques often encounter different capacity constraints and behavior as models scale to standard sizes (e.g., 7B/8B or 14B), leaving open questions regarding scalability.

Benchmark diversity and sequence length are limited. The experiments rely exclusively on the MRQA benchmark (primarily short-to-medium extractive reading comprehension passages partitioned into 510-token chunks). To support claims about handling vast, long contexts, evaluations on dedicated long-context benchmarks (such as LongBench, L-Eval, or RULER) spanning summarization, multi-hop reasoning, and retrieval tasks are needed.

The paper lacks real-world inference efficiency measurements. While compression ratios are reported, there is no wall-clock latency, throughput, or peak GPU memory benchmarking during inference to quantify practical gains over full-context inference or KV cache compression baselines.

Minor presentation issues, including an incomplete sentence and missing anonymous code repository link in Section 7 ('supplementary material: This code can be used...'), and occasional typos (e.g., 'inferenece' on page 2).

strengths: Clear motivation: Context compression architectures traditionally rely on autoencoding (AE) pretraining to imbue randomly initialized compression tokens with meaning. The paper convincingly argues that AE training incurs high computational cost and creates an objective mismatch with downstream usage.

Well-motivated and clean architecture: Semantic-Anchor Compression (SAC) selects contextual tokens directly as anchors, adds anchor embeddings to mark them, and applies bidirectional attention to aggregate context across the input sequence without needing autoencoding reconstruction.

Strong empirical improvements: SAC consistently outperforms competitive baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, and LLMLingua-2) across various compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x) on both in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA benchmarks.
Efficient pretraining: Eliminating the AE objective reduces pretraining time by ~26-31% while achieving lower LM perplexity.

Detailed ablation and analysis: The paper includes informative ablations on anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention, anchor selection strategies, and representation analysis (attention maps and t-SNE).
weaknesses: Limited model scale: Experiments are conducted exclusively on Llama-3.2-1B. Evaluating whether these conclusions and performance gains hold on standard 7B/8B models would significantly strengthen the paper.

Narrow benchmark diversity: Evaluation is restricted almost entirely to question answering on MRQA datasets. It remains unclear how well SAC performs on broader long-context benchmarks (e.g., LongBench, L-Eval, or summarization/code understanding tasks).

Short context window regime: The context is chunked into sub-contexts of 510 tokens, and MRQA passages are relatively short (hundreds to low thousands of tokens). True long-context settings (8k-32k+ tokens) are not demonstrated.

Incremental technical novelty: The individual components (uniform anchor selection following EPL, bidirectional attention adaptation from LLM2Vec/NV-Embed, and token embeddings) are largely adaptations of existing concepts, though their synthesis for context compression is neat.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: The critique of autoencoding (AE) pretraining as computationally expensive and potentially misaligned with downstream tasks is well-founded. The paper provides insightful gradient orthogonality analysis between AE and LM objectives (Figure 9) to justify dispensing with AE training.

Clean and practical method: Repurposing contextual tokens as compression carriers via anchor embeddings and full bidirectional attention is an elegant design that avoids sequence length expansion and eliminates learning soft compression tokens from scratch.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly evaluated against several strong recent baselines (e.g., ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL) across multiple compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x), different model scales (1B, 3B, 8B), and multiple downstream settings (in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA, 24K long-context QA, and 32K summarization).

Detailed analysis and ablations: The paper provides extensive ablation studies validating each component (bidirectional attention, anchor embedding, token selection strategy, objective choices), as well as informative representation (t-SNE) and attention map visualizations.
weaknesses: Overstated scalability claims on 8B models: The text in Section 4.4 asserts that 'as the model goes larger, the gain does not seem to diminish'. However, inspecting the 8B in-domain results in Table 18 reveals that SAC (67.09 F1 / 51.08 EM) is virtually identical to EPL (67.08 F1 / 50.60 EM), and actually underperforms EPL on several individual subsets (SQuAD, NewsQA, TriviaQA). The paper should discuss these scaling nuances more transparently.

Moderate architectural novelty: Conceptually, the work builds heavily upon EPL (Zhao et al., 2025), replacing EPL's interleaved soft tokens with context tokens plus an indicator embedding and bidirectional attention. While the combination is effective, the technical jump is somewhat incremental.

Simplistic anchor selection: The default strategy simply takes the middle token of each uniform chunk. Although comparisons with LLMLingua-2 and random selection are provided in Table 4, more comprehensive investigations into content-aware or query-aware selection strategies would strengthen the framework's positioning.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper challenges the conventional autoencoding (AE) pretraining paradigm established by prior context compression frameworks (such as ICAE and 500xCompressor), providing both intuitive and gradient-level evidence that the token reconstruction objective can conflict with language modeling and downstream tasks.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span multiple benchmarks including in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA subsets, long-context QA (up to 24K tokens), and long-document summarization (QMSum, GovReport up to 32K tokens), consistently demonstrating strong or competitive performance across compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x).

Detailed ablation and diagnostic studies: The authors provide thorough ablations on anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention masks, token selection strategies, and training objectives (AE vs. LM), alongside insightful representation analysis (t-SNE of KV cache, gradient cosine similarity, and attention map visualizations).

Efficiency benefits: By directly leveraging contextual positions and eliminating extra compression tokens as well as the computationally intensive autoencoding pretraining phase, the method achieves lower training overhead and reduced inference FLOPs compared to soft-token baselines.
weaknesses: Conceptual tension in the 'semantic' naming and token selection: Table 4 reveals that selecting arbitrary middle tokens uniformly from chunks performs slightly better than or on par with an information-entropy-based selector (Lingua-2: 63.63 vs. 63.26 F1 on ID; 47.72 vs. 47.43 F1 on OOD). This suggests that the compression capability may stem predominantly from uniform positional pooling and bidirectional contextual aggregation rather than the intrinsic lexical/semantic importance of the chosen anchor tokens.

Mixed scalability trends at the 8B parameter scale: While the paper claims gains do not diminish as model size increases, Table 18 shows that for Llama-3.1-8B on in-domain QA, SAC achieves an average F1 of 67.09 compared to EPL's 67.08 (virtually identical), and underperforms EPL on certain tasks such as SQuAD and NewsQA, as well as on BioASQ in out-of-domain evaluation (Table 19: 48.54 vs. 52.52 F1).

Incremental architectural novelty: The individual components—bidirectional attention in decoder-only LLM encoders (e.g., LLM2Vec, NV-Embed), uniform token spacing across chunks (e.g., EPL), and indicator prompt/anchor embeddings—are largely existing concepts adapted together to replace dedicated soft compression tokens.

Minor presentation and formatting errors: The draft contains several typos and formatting artifacts (e.g., missing repository URLs in the Abstract and Reproducibility statement, 'compressd' on page 2, and 'Sigle-Doc-Avg' in Table 21).

strengths: Clear motivation and insightful critique of existing soft prompt compression paradigms: the paper systematically demonstrates that autoencoding (reconstruction) pretraining objectives can cause gradient conflicts with language modeling and downstream task objectives.

Well-motivated and effective architecture: replacing randomly initialized soft tokens with selected contextual anchor tokens, augmented by bidirectional attention and anchor embeddings, leverages natural semantic priors and improves compression efficiency.

Extensive empirical evaluation: experiments cover 12 MRQA datasets (both in-domain and out-of-domain), three compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x), three model sizes (Llama-3.2-1B, 3B, and Llama-3.1-8B), as well as 24K/32K long-context summarization and QA benchmarks, consistently demonstrating gains over strong baselines like EPL and 500xCompressor.

Thorough analytical support: the paper provides comprehensive ablation studies, gradient cosine similarity analyses, theoretical FLOPs, wall-clock latency benchmarks, attention map visualizations, and t-SNE representation analyses.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty relative to EPL: the method builds directly upon the uniform position distribution strategy of EPL, primarily modifying it by anchoring onto existing context tokens rather than inserted soft tokens, alongside standard bidirectional masking.

Superficial exploration of anchor selection strategies: uniform middle-token selection performs on par with the entropy-distilled LLMLingua-2 selection, but the paper offers limited theoretical or empirical insight into why sophisticated semantic selection does not outperform simple uniform chunking.

Scope of long-context and scaling evaluations: while MRQA is tested across 1B, 3B, and 8B models, the long-context summarization (32K) and QA (24K) benchmarks are restricted to the 1B model, leaving open questions about long-context scaling behavior.
Minor presentation issues: incomplete sentences/placeholders in the Abstract and Section 7 where repository URLs were omitted (e.g., 'released at ' without an anonymous link or placeholder text).
